## Messengers and offers

**Messengers are errands (decided 21 October 2026).** Word from abroad needs someone to carry it. A report or letter from an envoy, a spy or anyone else comes home only with a carrier: someone hired ("Anyone can hire anyone"), a traveller going that way, such as a merchant carrying letters on the side, or the person himself travelling home. Nothing arrives by itself. Carrying is an errand like any other (deliver a letter or a tablet, bring back a reply), so the messenger needs no role of his own.

- **Envoy or messenger.** An envoy has a mandate and an audience and can bargain. A messenger only delivers and brings back an answer: cheaper and quicker to find, but with no authority, so a king chooses between them for each errand. The sources draw the same line: Arzawa's king would not trust what Pharaoh's messenger said until a tablet confirmed it.
- **Word from abroad is a decision.** An envoy kept waiting or detained must choose how to get word home ("they are holding me", "the king asks for more", "shall I seal?"): hire someone at that court, trust a passing merchant, or send one of his own people. A spy's report needs a carrier too, so every report carries risk: the carrier can be intercepted, questioned or bribed, and lead back to the spy.
- **The carrier has motives of his own.** He can read what he carries if he knows its language, sell what it says, swap it for a forgery ("Swapped tablets"), lose it to bandits on the road, or deliver it faithfully because his name is his living. These are errors with motives, as pillar 3 asks.
- **No faceless channel (decided 21 October 2026).** Nothing is sent without someone, not even more slowly and with a greater chance of loss. Everything that can happen to a letter comes from its carrier, so a lost tablet is a story with someone to blame, bribe or suspect, not a roll of the dice; history had no such channel either, which is why kings complained of their messengers being held for years at a foreign court. The reason in the game is language: a tablet must be accompanied by talk. A letter was read aloud at court and its bearer questioned; he said what the tablet left unsaid and took the answer home, the tablet confirming his words ("Envoy or messenger"), and how well he is understood follows the language system ("Languages"). Soldiers and porters do not speak the language of a foreign court and are not received by its king, so an army or a caravan can carry goods but never a letter. Handing over goods needs no language (this for that can be done by gesture, as in the silent trade Herodotus describes), but bargaining is talk, so a caravan only delivers what its orders say, while a character leading it can strike a bargain. Inside a realm, orders and reports travel with the realm's own couriers, men in a unit like caravans rather than named characters, since they speak the realm's own language ("Distance inside your own realm").
- **Side jobs on the road.** Those in a city see who has arrived there, so anyone may offer a passing traveller a fee to carry a tablet, and the offer wakes him ("Characters sleep like kings"): at most one call at a stop where someone wants something. A stranger is slow, since he keeps his own road and schedule; unreliable, since he owes the sender nothing; and cheap, since he is paid for a favour on his way, not for a journey of his own. An envoy who carries for others serves two masters: Egypt's envoy taking Aziru's letter to Hatti can open it or sell it to his own king, so envoys on the road are among the best sources of intelligence in the game, and senders must choose their carriers with care. A well-paid delivery off his road delays his king's mission, and the king learns of it only when the news reaches him: he can notice side jobs, not forbid them, as with skimming.
- **Paid on delivery.** Half now and the rest from the recipient is the natural safeguard. Nothing enforces it, so it rests on reputation, like every other debt.
- **Forgery needs a skill; betrayal does not.** Most carriers cannot read Akkadian, so a passing merchant can rarely falsify what he carries, but he can sell it to someone who can, or pay a scribe to read it. The road is where the risk lies: in EA 8 Burna-Buriash complains to Pharaoh that his merchants were robbed and killed in Canaan, and asks for redress.
- **The rest emerges.** Fees, speed and trust come out of play: a carrier known for delivering faithfully can ask more, merchants on busy roads carry letters cheaply, and relay stations (build order item 15) make carriers faster.
- **Every seat uses it.** Script envoys and spies decide when to send word and whom to trust with it, and script carriers decide by their traits whether to read, sell or swap what they carry ("Every feature is every seat's").

In build order item 7 news already travels with people along the route; until item 11b, a report travels that route by itself, as if the engine carried it. From item 11b it needs a real carrier ("Messengers are errands").

**Offers made in words.** Gold and land move only by engine orders: an offer counts as a payment only when gold is handed over at the audience, as bribes already are, or later through a structured promise. A spoken offer ("fifty shekels if you soften your report") moves nothing, like a promise typed in chat in Civilization beside an empty trade window. Whether the character believes it and acts on it is its own judgement; the host may pay later, or not, and the character has bet on a king's word. Script characters cannot read free text, so they answer by formula to the clauses every letter carries, and when the character layer is set to script bots every king writes only from the templates ("Two press modes"). No extraction pass is needed.
